## Background
Genesis is traditionally attributed to Moses. Many scholars think it was gathered from several sources over time and reached its final form around the 500s BC. Verses 1–3 complete the seven-day creation account of chapter 1. From verse 4 the story starts again in a different style. God is now called "the LORD God," joining God's personal name to the general word for God, and he is shown working closely with his hands: forming, planting and breathing. Some readers see two separate accounts. Others see the same creation retold from closer up, focused on human beings. Either way, Israel's first readers would have heard here how they and all people came to be.

## What happens
The chapter opens with completion. God finishes his work, rests on the seventh day, and blesses and sanctifies it, setting it apart as holy (vv. 1–3).

A new account begins with the earth still bare. Nothing grows yet because there is no rain and no one to till the ground, though a mist waters the land (vv. 4–6). Then the LORD God forms the man from the dust of the ground and breathes into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man becomes a living being (v. 7).

God plants a garden in Eden, full of trees that are beautiful and good to eat. In the middle stand the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (vv. 8–9). A river flows out of Eden and divides into four, two of which, the Hiddekel (Tigris) and the Euphrates, were well known to ancient readers (vv. 10–14).

God places the man in the garden to work it and keep it (v. 15). He gives generous freedom to eat from every tree, with one exception. The man must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, or he will die (vv. 16–17).

For the first time something is "not good": the man is alone (v. 18). God brings the animals to him, and he names them, but none is a fitting partner (vv. 19–20). So God puts the man into a deep sleep, takes a rib, and builds a woman (vv. 21–22). The man responds with joy: "bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (v. 23). The narrator adds that a man will leave his parents and cleave to his wife, and the two become one flesh (v. 24). They are naked and unashamed (v. 25).

## Key words and ideas
- Dust and breath: in Hebrew the man is adam, formed from the adamah, the ground. Humans are earthy and fragile, yet they live by God's own breath.
- Help meet: the Hebrew ezer kenegdo means a helper "corresponding to" or "fit for" him. Ezer is used elsewhere of God helping Israel, so it does not mean an inferior. Christians differ on what this chapter implies for the roles of men and women.
- Two trees: the tree of life points to the life God offers. The forbidden tree marks the limit of human freedom, where people must trust God's word.
- One flesh: a union of whole lives. Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand marriage as a sacrament, while most Protestants describe it as a sacred covenant.

## Connections
Hebrews 4:4 points to God's seventh-day rest as a picture of the rest God offers his people. Jesus says in Mark 2:27 that the Sabbath was made for man. Ecclesiastes 12:7 echoes verse 7: dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God. Paul calls Christ "the last Adam," a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45). The tree of life reappears as a promise in Revelation 2:7. Jesus quotes verse 24 when he teaches on marriage and divorce (Matthew 19:3–9). Ephesians 5:28–31 applies it to Christ and the church.

## For reflection
- What does it mean to you that you are made of dust yet alive by God's breath?
- How do you respond to God's generosity ("freely eat") alongside his one limit?
- Where in your life do you see that "it is not good" to be alone?
